parts.note: the Dickens title read literally: what fills a shop selling old curios is a jumble of small ornaments and knick-knacks

explanation.surface: A table of contents for the Dickens novel The Old Curiosity Shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like a book title and its chapter list; read plainly, it asks what a curiosity shop actually holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted ornaments and trinkets of little value are exactly the stock of a curiosity shop.

definitions.meaning: sailing vessels, an old spelling of barques
dogs that bay give voice loudly, as when they yap

explanation.definitionFit: The word names three-masted sailing vessels and also what a dog does when it gives voice.

parts.note: the proverb calls necessity the mother of ..., so the child of necessity

explanation.surface: A child born into poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Necessitous' looks like 'needy'; read as 'of Necessity', it points to the proverb 'Necessity is the mother of invention'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb makes necessity the parent and a new contrivance its child.

parts.note: the Roman goddess of the dawn is a woman, and also the polar glow in the night sky

explanation.surface: A woman of loose morals, or a slender one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light woman' is an old phrase for a wanton; here the goddess of dawn shares her name with the northern and southern lights, and is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both the Roman dawn goddess and the glowing lights seen near the poles.

definitions.meaning: small deer, cud-chewers, as the plural of the roe deer
fish eggs, spawn in a mass

explanation.definitionFit: The word is the plural of a small deer, a cud-chewing animal, and also masses of fish spawn.

parts.note: a tree hung with lights stands in for the Christmas fir, and there is also a tropical plant of that name

explanation.surface: Something to use instead of a Christmas tree.
explanation.walkthrough: A tropical tree bearing candle-like fruit has this name; the clue pictures it standing in for the candlelit Christmas fir.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree hung with tapers, or the tropical tree whose fruit resembles tapers, could replace the festive fir.

clue.text: Bit-part for him in " Vice Versa

definitions.text: Bit-part for him in " Vice Versa

parts.words: Bit-part for him in " Vice Versa
parts.note: the proverb says the one who does the biting ends up bitten; with roles swapped he gets the 'bit' part

explanation.surface: An actor landing a small role in the comic novel and play Vice Versa.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'the biter bit' describes a schemer caught by his own trick; 'Vice Versa' (also an F. Anstey title about father and son swapping places) signals the role reversal, so he plays the one who is 'bit'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'the biter bit' names someone who intends harm and suffers it, so he is cast as the bitten party.

parts.note: a horse-drawn closed carriage named after the Victorian Lord Chancellor who designed it

explanation.surface: The dignified bearing of a statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carriage' suggests posture; it is a vehicle named after Henry Brougham, the 19th-century statesman and Lord Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: The four-wheeled one-horse closed carriage takes its name from Lord Brougham, a Victorian politician.

parts.note: one who tests or tries things, and also a German city standing on the Moselle river

explanation.surface: An irritable man complaining about a German wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Testy' looks like 'irritable'; read as 'one who tests', it gives the word for someone who tries, which is also an ancient German city on the Moselle.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who makes attempts or tests is a tester, and the same word names the old Roman city beside the Moselle.

clue.text: Order of the garter, sir, for a marrying man

indicators.note: the letters of the words are put into a fresh order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A knight of the Order of the Garter, addressed as sir, who is keen to wed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order of the garter' looks like the chivalric order; 'Order of' signals rearranging GARTER and SIR.
explanation.definitionFit: The official at a register office conducts civil weddings, so he marries people.

clue.text: Wearer of dog-collar, Gaelic, the other way round

parts.note: a clergyman in a clerical collar is a Reverend, abbreviated Rev
Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: A Gaelic-speaking clergyman who does everything backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end and reads like a description of the priest; it is a phrase meaning 'backwards'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in the opposite direction or order is turning it about, a synonym for the definition phrase.

clue.text: What 19 saw the Hunter doing to the Sultan's turret

definitions.text: What 19 saw the Hunter doing to the Sultan's turret

parts.words: What 19 saw the Hunter doing to the Sultan's turret
parts.note: a line from the Rubaiyat: 'the Hunter of the East has caught the Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light'

explanation.surface: A poet watching a huntsman lasso the tower of a Sultan's palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is the Persian poet of the Rubaiyat; in FitzGerald's translation the dawn, the Hunter of the East, catches the Sultan's turret in a noose of light, so the Hunter is snaring it with a loop.
explanation.definitionFit: Catching something in a running loop of rope is lassoing it, the action the poem's Hunter performs on the turret.

clue.text: He takes a box, but has to stand

definitions.text: He takes a box, but has to stand

parts.words: He takes a box, but has to stand
parts.note: a guard on duty occupies a small sentinel's hut yet stays on his feet

explanation.surface: A theatregoer who books a box but still ends up standing.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'box' suggests the theatre, where a box comes with seats; the guard's box is a sentry box, where he stands watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier posted on guard keeps watch from a small hut and remains standing on duty.

clue.text: Ladies who no longer come to terms

definitions.text: Ladies who no longer come to terms

parts.words: Ladies who no longer come to terms
parts.note: former pupils of a girls' school have finished attending its school terms

explanation.surface: Women who have stopped reaching agreements in a dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to terms' looks like reaching agreement; here the terms are school terms, which past pupils no longer attend.
explanation.definitionFit: Former pupils of a girls' school are its alumnae, no longer turning up each term.

parts.note: a number expressed out of every hundred, as rates and proportions are

explanation.surface: An exclamation about someone who is one in a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A figure in a hundred' sounds like 'one in a hundred'; it is a figure expressed per hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: A proportion stated per hundred is a rate out of a hundred.

definitions.meaning: a garden plant with sword-shaped leaves, also called flag
a seer is one who sees, and the coloured ring of the eye is part of what sees

explanation.definitionFit: It names both a bloom of the flag family and the coloured disc of the eye that serves anyone who sees.

clue.text: To the extent that an African prince is given Ottoman asylum ?

parts.note: an ottoman is a sofa, so refuge in an ottoman is being in a sofa
Ras is an Ethiopian title for a prince or chief

explanation.surface: An Ethiopian prince granted refuge by the Ottoman Empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ottoman' looks like the Turkish empire; it is the couch, so the prince sheltering 'in sofa' gives IN SOFA plus RAS.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'as far as' or 'to the degree that', a connective of extent.

parts.note: sinister is Latin for left, and a bat in cricket is a batsman, so a batsman who plays from the left side

explanation.surface: A menacing winged creature of the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinister' looks like 'evil' and 'bat' like the animal; sinister is heraldic and Latin for 'left', and in cricket a bat is a batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman who bats with his left hand lower on the handle is a southpaw at the crease.

parts.note: unable to speak is dumb
a painting or picture is art
a film showing is on

explanation.surface: A silent film being screened at a cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No talking picture' suggests a silent film; the pieces are DUMB, ART and ON, and 'here' points to a place: the Scottish town on the Clyde.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish town on the Clyde is a place, so 'here' stands for it.

clue.text: Chastisement to make one see stars

definitions.text: Chastisement to make one see stars

parts.words: Chastisement to make one see stars
parts.note: a biblical lash used for punishment, and a constellation of the zodiac in the stars

explanation.surface: A beating so hard it leaves the victim seeing stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See stars' looks like being dazed by a blow; in 1 Kings 12 Rehoboam chastises with whips of this name, and it is also a zodiac constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible it is a barbed whip for punishment, and in the sky it is a zodiac constellation.

clue.text: Is Daisy's tandem one of these ?

definitions.text: Is Daisy's tandem one of these ?

parts.words: Is Daisy's tandem one of these ?
parts.note: the song Daisy Bell is about a bicycle built for two, so its tandem is a bicycle in a song

explanation.surface: A question about a woman named Daisy and her two-seater bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song Daisy Bell ends 'on the seat of a bicycle made for two'; a tandem in a song is a punning 'song cycle', really a set of linked songs.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of songs meant to be performed in sequence as one work is a classical song series.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held is only 'See 10': the poet is named only by the reference '19' inside 10-across, which holds no definition or wordplay for this light.

parts.note: the Song of Solomon says 'stay me with flagons', so a guest who stays is like a flagon

explanation.surface: A visitor who resembles a drinking vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Song of Solomon (2:5) reads 'Stay me with flagons', making flagons things that stay; a guest who lingers is one too.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest who stays on, and a flagon that 'stays' in the biblical phrase, are both things that stay.

definitions.meaning: aggressive patriotism read as a '...', a ranting about the national flag

explanation.definitionFit: It means glaringly offensive, and split in two it is a rant about the flag, which is what jingoism amounts to.

parts.note: a cart that has been upset is far from steady, as in the idiom about upsetting a fruit cart

explanation.surface: A horse-drawn cart a long way from its stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like the horse's home; it means steady, and the idiom 'upset the apple cart' supplies the cart.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'upset the apple cart' means to spoil plans, and an upset cart is far from steady.

clue.text: Get thanks returned and forwarded on entry

indicators.note: the word for thanks is sent back, so it is read from right to left

parts.note: ta is an informal British way of saying thanks
the same ta again, this time forwarded, read the normal way
having entered, a person is in

explanation.surface: Getting a thank-you sent back and passed on as you come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thanks' is used twice: 'returned' reverses TA to AT, and 'forwarded' keeps the second TA as written.
explanation.definitionFit: To get or reach a goal is to achieve it, a synonym of the definition.

clue.text: Time being kept by musician on cello

indicators.note: the letters are held within the words that follow, kept inside them

explanation.surface: A cellist keeping time during a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time being kept' looks like a musician keeping time; 'kept by' tells you the answer is held inside 'musician on cello'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'For the time being' and 'for the present occasion' share the old phrase 'for the nonce'.

parts.note: a single droplet falling from a tap is the least amount of water that can fall

explanation.surface: The tiniest cascade in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waterfall' suggests a cascade; the smallest fall of water is a single drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop falling from a leaking tap is the least possible fall of water.

parts.note: something exactly like the original is a precise copy of it

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they like something, and replying emphatically.
explanation.walkthrough: The exchange reads as a question and an enthusiastic answer; run together it says 'like it exactly', a description of a copy.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact copy or reproduction resembles its original in every detail.

parts.note: the Sussex town name split into crow plus borough: a borough that gives its name to a crow

explanation.surface: A question mark over a town in East Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Crowborough is a real East Sussex town; split, it asks for a 'crow borough', a town in Hertfordshire that names the Royston crow, the hooded crow.
explanation.definitionFit: The hooded crow is called the Royston crow after the Hertfordshire town, making it a borough of crows.

parts.note: the Suffolk village name split as drink plus stone: a beer mug made of stoneware, and the German word for stone

explanation.walkthrough: Drinkstone is a real Suffolk village; split, a stoneware beer mug is a drink-stone, and the German word for 'stone' is the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A large earthenware beer mug, its name taken from the German for stone, holds drink and is made of stone.

clue.text: Shakespeare's hope of a rep scene

indicators.note: the hope is made of the letters of these words, rearranged; 'of' points to them as raw material

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean hope for a scene staged by a repertory company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' is the only signal: the answer is made of the letters of A REP SCENE. It is French for hope, the Percy family's battle-cry in Henry IV Part 1.
explanation.definitionFit: In Henry IV Part 1 Hotspur's cry is the French word for hope, the Percy motto.
